news_drafts.headline: Scottish Borders pension fund cash deficit widens as pensioners outnumber active members
news_drafts.lead: The Scottish Borders Council pension fund faces a structural cash deficit as pensioner numbers have grown to exceed active member numbers for the first time, with one pensioner now for every active member employed. Over the year to June 2026, pension payments and costs of £366m outstripped contributions by £9m, a shortfall the fund must cover from investment returns and reserves. Pensioner membership has risen 28% over five years while active members grew just 2.9%, a demographic shift that began when the fund matured in 2013/14. This year the fund delivered a 5.7% investment return, the lowest among Scotland's 11 local government pension schemes and well below its 12.3% benchmark; the fund has since terminated underperforming equity managers and committed to changes. Despite the cash flows, Audit Scotland's draft annual report concluded the fund has effective governance and financial management arrangements in place. The council's employer contribution rate was cut to 17% from 18.5% following a strong 134% funding valuation in 2023.

news_drafts.headline: Borders Pension Fund Reaches Maturity as Pensioners Outnumber Active Members
news_drafts.lead: The Scottish Borders Council pension fund has reached a structural turning point: the number of pensioners now exceeds active workers who contribute to it. With 5,487 pensioners against 4,839 active members—a shift accelerating over five years—the fund faces a permanent annual shortfall. Pension payments of £39.9m annually exceed new contributions of £28.9m by £11m, a gap the fund must cover from investment returns. The council reduced its employer contribution rate from 18.5% to 17% following a strong 2023 funding valuation, but recent investment performance has tested this approach. The fund returned 5.7% against a benchmark of 12.3%, the worst among 11 Scottish local authority pension schemes. Audit Scotland confirmed the fund maintains effective governance and financial sustainability, but it faces a permanent structural challenge as its membership ages.

findings.paper_title: Item No. 08 (c) - 2025-26 Lowood Tweedbank Limited accounts 31 March 2026
findings.headline: Company operates at perfect break-even with turnover matched exactly by costs in both years
findings.detail: In 2025/26, turnover of £49,952 is matched precisely by cost of sales of £49,952. The same break-even pattern occurred in 2024/25 (turnover £48,965; costs £48,965). The company accumulates no operating profit or reserves.
findings.matters: Perfect annual break-even suggests costs are absorbed elsewhere (by council staff and services) and the entity generates no financial surplus, leaving no operational margin for variation or contingency.
findings.quote: Operating Profit for the Financial Year -

findings.paper_title: Item No. 08 (c) - 2025-26 Lowood Tweedbank Limited accounts 31 March 2026
findings.headline: Subsidiary is minimally capitalized with net assets of only £1
findings.detail: The company has net assets of £1, with current assets of £37,339 offset almost entirely by current liabilities of £37,338 to the council. It holds no fixed assets. The £1 capital base provides negligible buffer against operational risks.
findings.matters: Minimal equity leaves the subsidiary with no financial cushion against adverse developments and suggests the council is managing it primarily through advances rather than capital investment.
findings.figures: Net assets £1; Current assets £37,339; Current liabilities £37,338

findings.paper_title: Item No. 08 (c) - 2025-26 Lowood Tweedbank Limited accounts 31 March 2026
findings.headline: Rental collection has improved substantially: arrears fell 57% to £2,500
findings.detail: Unpaid rental income decreased from £5,850 in 2024/25 to £2,500 in 2025/26, a reduction of £3,350. This represents improved collection performance on the housing program and reduces the council's financing burden through the subsidiary.
findings.matters: Better rent collection indicates the housing program is operationally performing and reduces the council's funding requirements for the subsidiary.

findings.paper_title: Item No. 08 (c) - 2025-26 Lowood Tweedbank Limited accounts 31 March 2026
findings.headline: Council's advances to subsidiary are being recovered: the debt owed fell by £11,287 to £37,338
findings.detail: The amount Scottish Borders Council has advanced to Lowood Tweedbank decreased from £48,625 in 2024/25 to £37,338 in 2025/26, a 23% reduction. This is the company's only liability, representing the council's deployment of capital to manage residential properties through a related entity.
findings.matters: A lender would want to understand the council's deployment of capital to related entities and whether that investment is being recovered or remains tied up.
findings.quote: Amounts owed to Scottish Borders Council 37,338

findings.headline: Integration Joint Board partnership with health board faces 'significantly challenging' financial sustainability.
findings.detail: Audit work on Scottish Borders Integration Joint Board (IJB)—consolidated into the council's group accounts—identified it does not have a formally documented Chief Finance Officer role, and faces limitations in risk oversight and strategic planning arrangements. More critically, audit concluded: 'Financial sustainability continues to be significantly challenging for the IJB.' This partnership is responsible for health and social care delivery in the council's area, a major budget area subject to political sensitivity.
findings.matters: A lender assessing group finances will be concerned about the viability of entities within the wider group. Poor financial health and limited governance in the IJB could create pressure on the council to provide additional funding or absorb unplanned costs, affecting council finances and reserves.
findings.figures: IJB is group component; chief finance officer arrangements not formally documented; multiple governance limitations identified
findings.quote: Financial sustainability continues to be significantly challenging for the IJB. These key messages were reported by the audit team to the IJB Audit Committee in September 2026.
